title: Make the *!*@?* animation! My experiences trying to get AI to create custom 3D animations
author: Aineisa
selftext:
Someone else in another post asked me to go into detail on my experiences trying to get good animations. I decided to do it as a separate post since I think many will find it useful. 

AI is good at doing non-biological, mechanical animations. Spider-robots, tank treads, pump stations, all good. 

I have has 0 success getting good natural, fluid, animations. 

Here’s what I’ve tried:  
\- custom designed tool. Built an AI tool pipeline that would query a few websites for motion-capped data. Get screenshots of the motions. Build the animation. Get screenshots of the animation in motion from all angles. Submit the results to several AI critics who compare it with the original mocap and return suggestions. 

This had bad-poor success. Human animations were passable but very stiff and unnatural. I wouldn’t use it. Trying to get a gorilla style walk-cycle was a total failure. 

\- Sorceress. Low-medium. You use the app to rig a model and then an AI to generate the anim. More natural looking than the previous attempt but getting cycles to loop is very difficult and no root motion, difficult to use controls, inconsistent results, meant I gave up trying to use it. 

\- meshy. Medium-good. Meshy has an animation library. Extremely limited. Needs way more animations to be useful. 

\- tripo3D. Bad-medium. I prefer Tripo over meshy in model generation but its animations are worse and auto-rigging is also worse than mixamo. The generated animations are sorceress quality or less. 

\- “AI? Make me an animation.” Low-medium. No fancy tools or products. Set Claude to a higher effort and let it work. Simple results like sitting, standing up after sitting, snakes, birds flapping wings, are ok. Action animations are not. 

\- voxel based animation. I paid money for this tool but gave up. It’s good for very simple models but once you have armour it becomes difficult to use since bones will pull other parts of the body. I’d rather use Blender.  

Conclusion:  
You can get good mechanical animations or simple natural movement animations but running, walking, anything with more action, is not good enough yet. 

I don’t think it’s impossible for AI to get some good animations but it’s too inconsistent for me. 

If someone wants a business idea here it is: create a huge, huge, library of blender animations. Sell it with an AI tool that takes in user input to parse the library, find good candidates and pass back to the user who selects one and can pass in a prompt for tweaks and adjustments to that library like “keep one hand in the air as if holding a torch” or “make the back more hunched as if carrying a very heavy object.”

comments.author: Ok-Leading8654
comments.body: Try BlendCap with SAM 3D Body, there's an installer if you feel like paying for it, otherwise it's up on github, SAM you get from huggingface, just request access! It's not flawless and you will need to clean up the motions a little bit, but as far as animations goes, it's by far the best I've found

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Oh, BlendCap looks interesting! Have you actually used it yourself?

How well does it handle running, jumping, foot contacts and more complicated movements? Does the resulting animation still need a lot of cleanup?

I have an RTX 5080 and have been experimenting with several motion-generation approaches, but the results often look stiff or unnatural.

Would love to hear what worked for you and what still needs fixing before I go down another rabbit hole, haha.

replies.author: Ok-Leading8654
replies.body:
I have actually used it! And I found that filming myself in 3/4 is a lot better than straight in front of me, or to the side. I've only done three animations with it thus far, been focusing on a few other things, but it's definitely the tool I'm going to be using going forward. And you'll have a great time with your 5080, I managed to get it running on my 1070 x).

I haven't tried running or jumping, thus far I've done an idle breathing animation, a whirlwind animation and an overhead slash animation. It's not flawless, I had Claude build some tools for me in blender to stabilize arms and make sure feet touch the ground, and an IK grip tool. So expect that anything you film will need a little bit of clean up, but all things considered it's like 15 minutes of work per animation once you've built the tooling to support it. I absolutely recommend giving it a go, good luck!

comments.author: FragmentedHeap
comments.body:
Yeah I have almost given up on the idea. 

What I'm exploring now is using VR tracking technology to try to track me and what I'm doing in a real space so that I can run and jump and stuff and record that and then translate it to a model.

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Thank you! I looked up MotionBricks and this actually looks very promising.

Have you tried it yourself? I am especially interested in its human animation and pose-to-pose transitions.

My game is a 2D side-scroller, but I can use 3D skeletal motion as a reference or retarget it onto a 2D rig.

Does it produce motion that can be exported and edited in Blender, or does it mainly work within its own runtime?

Would appreciate any practical experience you have with it!

replies.author: StoneCypher
replies.body:
no, it's brand new and i'm working on a 4x right now, so it doesn't really fit what i'm up to

it's just something i saw in the news which seemed like it might help

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Ah, fair enough! Thanks for pointing me towards it anyway. It definitely looks interesting, and I might investigate whether it can fit into my animation workflow.

Good luck with your 4X game, by the way! Appreciate the suggestion.

comments.author: taisui
comments.body: Might have been easier to record some video and have that converted into mocap animation then apply to the rig, instead trying to one shot it

comments.author: Bonelessgummybear
comments.body: I just had some great success with a custom animation with Claude and blender. Just guiding it step by step what I wanted to see

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
This is interesting because I have been trying something similar with Claude and Blender, but the animations often end up stiff.

Are you getting Claude to generate Python scripts that animate the rig directly? And what kind of animations have you managed to produce?

I am particularly interested in running, jumping, recoil and more expressive movements.

If you have any examples or tips on how you guide Claude through the poses, I would really appreciate them!

replies.author: Bonelessgummybear
replies.body: So I've put together a video I'm pretty proud of, showcasing the workflow step by step and the final result. I wanted to post it today but it got delayed just due to communication. It's for a sponsored post so I don't want to share it early. The specific animation is having my "creature" in a horror game block the back door with a fridge. I iterated with Claude to get a very realistic animation where the hand placement, bracing, weight shifting through hips, and the fridge slightly rotating while being pushed due to hand placement and physics. At the end, the animation got twisted so I used extra effort on opus to fix it for good. Very happy with the result and it made me realize I can get more advanced animations done

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Oh man, that actually sounds fantastic! Especially the hand placement, bracing and weight shifting. That is exactly the kind of physical detail I have been struggling to achieve.

No worries about the video, I completely understand. Would love to see it when it goes public!

One thing I am curious about: did Claude generate and modify the Blender animation directly through Python scripts, or were you using a specific rigging or animation tool?

And when you say you guided it step by step, were you describing the individual poses and body mechanics, or letting Claude figure those out from the scene?

I am wondering whether that approach could also work for running, jumping and weapon recoil, where timing and body weight matter so much.

Really appreciate you sharing this!

(P.S, do you mind dm'in me when you post it?)

replies.author: Bonelessgummybear
replies.body:
Give me a follow in case I forget to DM, I'm hoping I'm approved to post it on Monday. I can actually share with you the clip in the DMs. I generated and rigged the model in Tripo. Then brought the model into blender and used the MCP. I usually prefer letting Claude run blender headless but for this animation I knew I'd want to see it live and iterate quicker. I described the animation I wanted in detail. That was about 40% of the way there. Then I started correcting piece by piece. Lock out arms, position and brace, shift weight through hips, then keep the feet planted longer before next step because it almost looked like he was holding himself up in the air. 

I basically knew exactly what it should look like on my head. Spent around 10 minutes to nail the final animation. I definitely think you can apply the workflow for the animations you listed. I would find some frame data as a reference. Like 8 frame running animation for Claude to refer to. 

I'm really excited for cutscene possibilities now. Actually for my main project, I'm making a cinematic video of an intense action scene inside of blender.

comments.author: yaxir
comments.body:
Thank you for taking the time to write all this up! I genuinely appreciate it.

Your results sound painfully familiar. I have been experimenting with HY-Motion, Mixamo, Maya MotionMaker and 2D retargeting, and the biggest problem is still making the movements feel alive rather than mechanically correct.

One thing I am starting to wonder about is whether the problem lies in the animation timing itself. Strong key poses, anticipation, exaggerated movement and deliberate holds seem to matter much more than I originally realized.

Did you ever try taking the mocap results and deliberately exaggerating the important poses and timing, rather than trying to match the original motion exactly?

Also, your idea of a searchable animation library with AI-assisted modifications makes so much sense. I would genuinely love something like that.

Thanks again for sharing your experience!

replies.author: Aineisa
replies.body:
Exaggerating could work but I’m not sure it would be enough.

If I was to try again I’d maybe try my original solution but with double the amount of reference images from different angles for AI agents to critique.

comments.author: Mother_Tifa
comments.body: I think animation consistency is still one of the biggest challenges with AI-generated 3D assets...

comments.author: Bloodywanker231
comments.body:
Have you looked into inverse kinematics with procedural animations.

You have your agent build an internal test environment in which you have it test the IK solver to then generate movement or animations. You could run realtime solvers or record the animations. Doesn't apply to every use case but still a powerful tool.
